'''''Quercus canariensis''''', the '''Algerian oak''', '''Mirbeck's oak''' or '''zean oak''', is an [[oak]] native to southern [[Portugal]], [[Spain]], [[Tunisia]], [[Algeria]] and [[Morocco]]. Despite the scientific name, it does not occur naturally today in the [[Canary Islands]].<ref name="ThePlantList" /> It is placed in [[Quercus sect. Quercus|section ''Quercus'']].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Denk |first1=Thomas |last2=Grimm |first2=Guido W. |last3=Manos |first3=Paul S. |last4=Deng |first4=Min |last5=Hipp |first5=Andrew L. |date=2017-11-02 |title=Appendix 2.1: An updated infrageneric classification of the oaks |website=figshare |doi=10.6084/m9.figshare.5547622.v1 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Appendix_2_1_________An_updated_infrageneric_classification_of_the_oaks/5547622/1 |access-date=2023-02-17 |format=xls |name-list-style=amp |mode=cs1}}</ref>

==Description==
''Quercus canariensis'' is a medium-sized [[deciduous]] to [[Semi-deciduous|semi-evergreen]] [[tree]] growing to {{Convert|20–30|m|abbr=off}} tall with a trunk up to {{Convert|1.5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in diameter. The [[leaves]] are {{Convert|10–15|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long and 6–8 cm broad, with 6–12 pairs of shallow lobes. The [[flower]]s are [[catkin]]s; the [[fruit]] is an [[acorn]] 2.5 cm long and 2 cm broad, in a shallow cup.<ref>{{Flora Europaea |genus=Quercus |species=canariensis}}</ref>

The tree is a recipient of the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/14244/Quercus-canariensis/Details | title = ''Quercus canariensis'' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 17 February 2021}}</ref>

==Landmark specimens==
[[Image:Algerian Oak.JPG|left|thumb|Algerian oak]]
Grand old Algerian oak tree was planted on 19 May 1863. It resides within the Kyneton Botanical Gardens in the town of [[Kyneton]] in the [[Australia|Australian]] state of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]]. This tree is listed by the National Trust on the Register of Significant Trees in Victoria.
There are also two good specimens located in the Ballarat Botanical Gardens, one of which is believed to have been planted in 1920.
There was another significant old Algerian oak tree in Victoria at the [[Melbourne]] Royal Botanic Gardens. It was known as Lady Loch's Oak; its trunk split in half in November 2007, due to the weight of its giant old limbs. The tree has been extensively planted in Canberra.

There are over a dozen mature trees in [[St Vincent Gardens]], [[Albert Park, Victoria]], some possibly dating back to the late 19th to early 20th century.
